---
title: "Network types"
description: >
  Every configuration of a net_frame, from a one-mode network to
  multilayer, temporal, spatial, ego, and partially observed networks:
  the tables, the net_frame() call, the printed card, and a plot that
  makes the configuration visible.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96)
```

Every network in knappnet is two data frames, one row per node and one row
per edge. What kind of network it is (directed or not, two-mode,
weighted, multiplex, temporal, spatial, and so on) is said by *roles*:
arguments of `net_frame()` that name the columns carrying structure, and
*declarations* that state properties the data must satisfy. This article
shows each configuration with its tables, the call, the card that
`print()` shows, and a plot. The [definitions](definitions.html) article
explains the choices behind each one, and `docs/DATA_MODEL.md` in the
repository is the full specification.

Most examples use the data sets shipped with the package
(`net_examples()` lists them, with their sources). Where a configuration
is not in any shipped data set, the example is *derived* from one, and
the text says how.

```{r}
library(knappnet)
net_examples()[, c("name", "type", "source")]
```

## Directed and undirected

Direction belongs to the network. Krackhardt's (1987) managers named the
colleagues they considered friends; the friendship ties are directed.

```{r}
friends <- net_example("krackhardt", relation = "friendship")
head(friends$edges)
friends
```

The same tables read as undirected make every named friendship mutual,
and a pair who named each other becomes two parallel edges (shown as
arcs):

```{r}
undirected <- net_frame(friends$edges, friends$nodes, directed = FALSE, source = "from",
                        target = "to", id = "name", quiet = TRUE)
undirected
```

```{r, fig.height = 4}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
xy <- plot(friends, main = "directed", node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
plot(undirected, layout = xy, main = "undirected", node_label = FALSE)
par(op)
```

## Two-mode networks

A two-mode network declares two disjoint sets of nodes, and every edge
joins one to the other. Davis, Gardner, and Gardner's (1941) women and
the social events they attended:

```{r}
women <- net_example("southern_women")
head(women$nodes)
head(women$edges)
women
```

`net_twomode()` is `net_frame()` with a `mode` column and the declaration
`between_modes_only = TRUE`; an edge within a mode is an error that lists
the rows. The plot puts each mode in its own row, and the projection onto
the women is an ordinary one-mode network:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(women, node_label = FALSE, main = "women and events")
plot(net_project(women), node_label = FALSE, main = "women, by shared events", seed = 1)
par(op)
```

## k-mode and multimode networks

A `mode` column may have any number of values. This three-mode network
is derived from the `country_borders` data: African countries belong to
subregions, and subregions to the continent, with edges only between
modes.

```{r}
cb <- net_example("country_borders")
africa <- cb$nodes[cb$nodes$continent == "Africa", ]
regions <- sort(unique(africa$subregion))
nodes <- data.frame(id = c(africa$code, regions, "Africa"),
                    mode = c(rep("country", nrow(africa)), rep("subregion", length(regions)),
                             "continent"))
edges <- data.frame(source = c(africa$code, regions),
                    target = c(africa$subregion, rep("Africa", length(regions))))
three <- net_frame(edges, nodes, directed = FALSE, mode = "mode", between_modes_only = TRUE)
three
plot(three, layout = "modes", node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

Adding the borders between countries makes a *multimode* network in the
sense of ORA: modes are declared, and ties within a mode are allowed
(`between_modes_only = FALSE`).

## Weighted networks: strength and distance

A weight column must say what it means. As a **strength** (frequency,
intensity), a larger weight brings nodes closer, and path-based measures
use 1/weight as the length; as a **distance** (cost, travel time), a
larger weight keeps them apart. The same three edges read both ways give
different shortest paths from `a` to `c`:

```{r}
w <- data.frame(source = c("a", "b", "a"), target = c("b", "c", "c"), w = c(1, 1, 5))
as_strength <- net_frame(w, directed = FALSE, weight = "w", weight_type = "strength")
as_distance <- net_frame(w, directed = FALSE, weight = "w", weight_type = "distance")
as_strength
net_distances(as_strength)
net_distances(as_distance)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
xy <- plot(as_strength, main = "strength: a-c is strong", seed = 3)
plot(as_distance, layout = xy, main = "distance: a-c is far",
     edge_color = I(c("black", "black", "gray80")))
par(op)
```

Strengths are drawn wider the stronger the tie; distances do not change
the width, since a thick line would suggest a strong tie. Victor Hugo's
characters weighted by the chapters they share (Knuth 1993):

```{r}
mis <- net_example("les_miserables", weighted = TRUE)
mis
plot(mis, node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

## Signed networks

A `sign` column holds `-1` or `1`; a weight, if any, is the magnitude and
stays non-negative. Read's (1954) alliances and enmities among the
Gahuku-Gama subtribes; negative ties are dashed:

```{r}
tribes <- net_example("highland_tribes")
head(tribes$edges)
tribes
plot(tribes, seed = 1)
```

Signed values in one column, as Pajek and UCINET store them, are split by
`net_as_signed()`.

## Multiplex networks

Several relations on one node set, in one long edge table with a
`relation` column. Krackhardt's managers reported advice, friendship,
and reporting ties:

```{r}
krack <- net_example("krackhardt")
table(krack$edges$relation)
krack
plot(krack, node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

Edges of different relations are never parallel, so this network is
simple. Each relation can also be drawn on its own, with a shared layout:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
xy <- net_layout(krack, seed = 1)
relations <- net_split_relations(krack)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (r in names(relations)) plot(relations[[r]], layout = xy, main = r, node_label = FALSE)
par(op)
```

## Multilayer networks

Actors stay in the node table; every edge names the layer of each
endpoint. An edge within a layer is intralayer; one joining an actor to
itself across layers is a coupling; any other edge across layers is
interlayer (Kivela et al. 2014). An optional layer table holds layer
attributes.

```{r}
edges <- data.frame(source = c("ann", "ann", "bob", "ann", "ann"),
                    target = c("bob", "bob", "cy", "ann", "cy"),
                    from_layer = c("work", "online", "online", "work", "work"),
                    to_layer = c("work", "online", "online", "online", "online"))
layers <- data.frame(layer = c("work", "online"), medium = c("office", "chat"))
ml <- net_frame(edges, directed = FALSE, source_layer = "from_layer",
                target_layer = "to_layer", layers = layers)
ml
cbind(edges, net_edge_layers(ml)["class"])
```

A multiplex network is the special case whose only edges between layers
are couplings. `net_as_multilayer()` lifts one, here Krackhardt's three
relations with a coupling between every pair of layers, and
`net_plot_layers()` draws one panel per layer:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
krack_layers <- net_as_multilayer(krack)
krack_layers
net_plot_layers(krack_layers, node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

## Temporal networks

Edges carry times in one of three forms: a `start` alone makes each edge
an instantaneous **contact**, `start` and `end` make it a half-open
**spell** `[start, end)`, and a whole-number `wave` puts it in a panel
wave `[k, k + 1)`. Times may be numbers, dates, or date-times.

### Contacts

```{r}
calls <- data.frame(source = c("a", "b", "a", "c", "b", "d", "a"),
                    target = c("b", "c", "c", "d", "d", "a", "d"),
                    time = c(1, 2, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8))
contacts <- net_frame(calls, directed = FALSE, start = "time")
contacts
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
net_plot_timeline(contacts)
net_plot_snapshots(contacts, width = 3, seed = 1)
```

### Edge spells and node spells

Two spells of one tie are two rows, not parallel edges. Nodes may have
presence spells too, as two columns (one spell each) or as a long table
(several spells per node); an edge must fall within the presence of both
endpoints.

```{r}
spells <- data.frame(source = c("ann", "ann", "bob", "cy"),
                     target = c("bob", "bob", "cy", "dee"),
                     from = c(0, 12, 3, 6), to = c(10, 15, 9, 14))
people <- data.frame(id = c("ann", "bob", "cy", "dee"), joined = c(0, 0, 2, 5),
                     left = c(NA, NA, NA, 16))
stream <- net_frame(spells, people, directed = FALSE, start = "from", end = "to",
                    node_start = "joined", node_end = "left")
stream
net_plot_snapshots(stream, breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12, 16), seed = 1)
```

Nodes absent from a window are drawn light gray. Several spells per node
and attributes that change over time go in the `node_spells` and
`node_changes` tables (see `?net_node_spells`).

### Panels

Sampson's (1968) novices ranked whom they liked at three times. Each
wave is the spell `[k, k + 1)`:

```{r}
liking <- net_example("sampson", relation = "liking")
liking
net_plot_snapshots(liking, node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

A panel can also be derived from contacts: cut the contact times into
windows and stack the windows as waves. Here the contacts above become
two waves:

```{r}
waves <- net_snapshots(contacts, breaks = c(1, 5, 9))
panel <- net_panel(waves)
panel
sapply(net_waves(panel), function(g) nrow(g$edges))
```

## Spatial networks

Nodes with coordinates (or sf geometry) make a spatial network;
adjacency still comes from the edge table. A spatial network is drawn on
its coordinates. Road distances between cities in the north-eastern
United States, derived from the `miles` data by keeping cities in nine
states and pairs at most 120 miles apart:

```{r}
miles <- net_example("miles")
ne <- miles$nodes[miles$nodes$state %in% c("ME", "NH", "VT", "MA", "RI", "CT", "NY", "NJ",
                                           "PA"), ]
near <- miles$edges[miles$edges$from %in% ne$name & miles$edges$to %in% ne$name &
                      miles$edges$miles <= 120, ]
roads <- net_frame(near, ne, directed = FALSE, source = "from", target = "to", id = "name",
                   weight = "miles", weight_type = "distance",
                   coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), quiet = TRUE)
roads
plot(roads, node_label = FALSE)
```

Country borders, with each country at its representative point:

```{r}
cb
plot(cb, node_label = FALSE)
```

## Spatio-temporal networks

Spatial and temporal roles together give a `spatiotemporal_net_frame`.
No shipped data set has both, so this one is derived from the
north-eastern road network above by giving each link a time equal to its
length: the panels then show the short, middle, and long links on the
map.

```{r}
banded <- near
banded$band <- banded$miles
st <- net_frame(banded, ne, directed = FALSE, source = "from", target = "to", id = "name",
                start = "band", coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), quiet = TRUE)
class(st)
st
net_plot_snapshots(st, breaks = c(0, 60, 90, 121), layout = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                   node_label = FALSE)
```

## Ego networks

An `ego` column on nodes and edges holds a collection of ego networks in
one net_frame, as egocentric surveys collect them. They can also be
derived from a whole network: here the first-order advice networks of
three of Krackhardt's managers.

```{r}
advice <- net_example("krackhardt", relation = "advice")
egos <- net_ego_frame(advice, egos = c(2, 7, 21), threads = 1)
egos
head(egos$nodes)
net_plot_egos(egos, node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

`net_split_egos()` returns one network per ego, and `net_to_egor()` and
`as_net_frame()` convert to and from egor's three tables.

## Missing data

An unobserved pair is a row flagged in a logical `edge_missing` column:
it is neither a tie nor a non-tie, is kept in the table, and is left out
of the graph that measures use. A non-respondent is a node flagged in a
logical `node_missing` column. In this example, derived from the
friendship network, managers 7 and 15 are treated as if they had not
answered, and two pairs as if they had not been asked about:

```{r}
fr_nodes <- friends$nodes
fr_nodes$no_reply <- fr_nodes$name %in% c(7, 15)
fr_edges <- friends$edges[!friends$edges$from %in% c(7, 15), ]
fr_edges$unknown <- FALSE
unasked <- data.frame(from = c(1, 3), to = c(5, 9), relation = "friendship",
                      unknown = TRUE)
fr_edges <- rbind(fr_edges, unasked)
partial <- net_frame(fr_edges, fr_nodes, source = "from", target = "to", id = "name",
                     node_missing = "no_reply", edge_missing = "unknown", quiet = TRUE)
partial
plot(partial, node_color = "no_reply", node_label = FALSE, seed = 1)
```

Measures refuse unresolved missing data. `net_resolve_missing()` makes
the choice explicit:

```{r}
net_density(net_resolve_missing(partial, "absent"))
```

## Self-loops and parallel edges

Loops and parallel edges are kept, counted on the card, and drawn: a loop
as a small circle, parallel edges as arcs. Two edges are parallel when
they share endpoints *and* relation, layers, and time spell.

```{r}
multi <- data.frame(source = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "c", "c"),
                    target = c("b", "b", "a", "c", "a", "a"),
                    calls = c(1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 1))
g <- net_frame(multi, weight = "calls", weight_type = "strength")
g
net_multiplicity(g)
simple <- net_simplify(g, remove_loops = TRUE)
simple
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
xy <- plot(g, main = "multigraph", seed = 2)
plot(simple, layout = xy, main = "simplified (weights summed)")
par(op)
```

Declaring `loops = FALSE` or `multiple = FALSE` turns each violating row
into an error that names it:

```{r, error = TRUE}
net_frame(multi, loops = FALSE, multiple = FALSE)
```

## Combining configurations

Roles combine freely: Sampson's data are directed, multiplex, signed, and
a panel at once, and the card says so.

```{r}
net_example("sampson")
```
